raw_case_text:
A 64-year-old male was admitted to our department as an emergency. He suffered from general malaise, fever, chills, and a pronounced nuchal and facial swelling on the left side. Since birth, he suffered from left-sided microtia with complete absence of meatus acusticus. His medical history was positive for diabetes mellitus type 2 treated by diet and an arterial hypertension controlled by 160 mg valsartan 160 mg/d.
On examination, we observed a left-sided head-and-neck edema with herpetiform-grouped vesicles around the left ear and on the nose and yellowish crusts and formation of bullae in the perioral region (Figures 1 and 2). Laboratory findings were remarkable for leukocytosis with a white blood cell count of 25.7 (normal range: 3.8-11.0), thrombocytopenia of 64 Gpt/L (120-340), lowered hematocrit of 0.245 L/L (0.40-0.54), hemoglobin of 5.1 mmol/L (8.6-12.1), erythrocyte count of 2.5 Tpt/L (4.6-6.2), neutrophilia of 13.8 Gpt/L (1.8-7.6), lymphopenia of 11% (20-45), increased number of large unstained cells with 2 Gpt/L (0-0.40), and C-reactive protein (CRP) of 333 mg/L (<5). HIV tests were negative.
Before submission, antibiotic treatment with sultamicillin was started and continued after submission at a dosage of 3 x 3 g/d intravenously (iv). The facial swelling, however, worsened. Therefore, the patient was referred to our Ear Nose Throat-department for diagnostics. Diagnostic ultrasound and thoracic computerized tomography (CT) were performed to exclude a bacterial or mycotic abscess formation.
With the diagnosis of impetiginized herpes zoster, antibiotic treatment was changed to 3 x 800 mg clindamycin/d plus aciclovir 3 x 500 mg/d. Pain management was realized using metamizole sodium 3 x 30 gtt/d. During the following days, only a minor clinical improvement was seen. In the peripheral blood, 11% blasts were noted. A bone marrow biopsy was suggested, but the patient refused.
The further course was characterized by malodorous oozing, formation of bullae, and increasing edema. On the left chin and left submandibular region, firm infiltrates were noted, and skin biopsies were taken to exclude specific infiltrates of a malignancy. Histopathology, however, was nonspecific, demonstrating only a putrid inflammation. Vesicles showed dissemination suggesting zoster generalisatus (Figures 3 and 4). Accordingly, we increased the dosage of aciclovir to 10 mg/kg (3 x 1000 mg/d) iv. The pain sensations become worse, and pregabalin was started in increasing doses. Certoparin sodium 3000 I.E. anti-Xa/d was injected subcutaneously for thrombosis prophylaxis.
Nevertheless, the situation did not improve. CRP increased to >400 mg/L, leukocytosis of 28.4 Gpt/L developed, and procalcitonin increased to 3.65 ng/mL (normal range: 0-0.5).
Under the suspicion of septicemia, we transferred the patient to the intensive care unit. Central venous access was realized by a subclavian catheter. The patient was treated by 4.5 g piperacillin, 500 mg levofloxacin, 1000 mg acyclovir every 8 hours, and initially 100 mg prednisolone. During the treatment course, he developed doughy stool; therefore, the antibiosis was changed to vancomycin 4 x 500 mg per os. Stool samples for Clostridium difficile remained negative. Clinical improvement was accompanied by reduction of vesiculation and edema.
After patient consent, CT and bone marrow biopsy were performed. Bone marrow analysis disclosed atypical myelopoiesis, reduced atypical erythropoiesis, and micromegakaryocytic megakaryopoiesis with 10% of bone marrow blasts confirming a myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS) refractory anemia and blast excess II (RAEB II). Chromosomal analysis and cytodiagnostics revealed a karyotype 46/XY and translocations t(2;12)(p13; q13) and t(6;9)(p22;q34). Due to anemia, erythrocyte concentrates were required.
Two weeks after admission, the patient suffered from pain in his right arm. The skin surrounding the subclavian catheter became erythematous. Therefore, the catheter was removed, but microbial cultures of the tip remained negative. Venous duplex sonography disclosed vena subclavia thrombosis and soft tissue hematoma.
In the following days, oozing of the scalp and the ear helix was observed. Microbial swaps identified Pseudomonas aeruginosa.
We intensified diuresis because of a progressive edema. Hemato-oncologist initiated cytoreductive treatment with azacitidine. Anemia and thrombocytopenia required erythrocyte and thrombocyte concentrates. Herpes zoster persisted. During intravenous infusion of varicella immunoglobulin, the patient developed an anaphylactic shock, which could be managed by intensive care. Six days later, the patient died due to a septic shock.
Written informed consent has been obtained from the patient before his tragic outcome to have the case details and any accompanying images published.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 64-year-old male presented as an emergency with acute left-sided facial and nuchal swelling, grouped periauricular/nasal vesicles, perioral bullae, fever, chills, and generalized malaise.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient developed acute left-sided head-and-neck edema accompanied by herpetiform vesicles around the left ear and nose, crusted perioral bullae, high fever, chills, and severe progressive pain that failed to respond to initial intravenous sultamicillin (3 x 3 g/day), clindamycin (3 x 800 mg/day), and standard-dose acyclovir (3 x 500 mg/day), progressing to generalized cutaneous dissemination (zoster generalisatus) and septicemia.
subjective.past_medical_history: Congenital left-sided microtia with complete external auditory canal atresia; diet-controlled type 2 diabetes mellitus; arterial hypertension.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for fever, chills, malaise, severe left facial/neck swelling and pain, and disseminated vesicular rash; developed right arm pain (subclavian thrombosis) and loose stools during hospitalization. Home medication: valsartan 160 mg/day.

objective.physical_examination: Marked left-sided head-and-neck edema, congenital left microtia with absent external auditory meatus, grouped herpetiform vesicles around the left ear and nose, yellowish crusts and bullae in the perioral region, firm indurated infiltrates over the left chin and submandibular area, and subsequent generalized vesicular dissemination across the body with malodorous oozing of the scalp and ear helix.
objective.routine_investigations: Admission labs showed marked leukocytosis (WBC 25.7 Gpt/L, rising to 28.4 Gpt/L; reference 3.8–11.0), neutrophilia (13.8 Gpt/L; reference 1.8–7.6), lymphopenia (11%; reference 20–45%), 11% peripheral blood blasts, large unstained cells 2 Gpt/L, severe normocytic anemia (hemoglobin 5.1 mmol/L [reference 8.6–12.1], hematocrit 0.245 L/L, RBC 2.5 Tpt/L), thrombocytopenia (platelets 64 Gpt/L; reference 120–340), markedly elevated CRP (333 mg/L, rising to >400 mg/L; reference <5), elevated procalcitonin (3.65 ng/mL; reference 0–0.5), and negative HIV testing. Stool C. difficile testing was negative; scalp and ear helix swabs grew Pseudomonas aeruginosa. Venous duplex ultrasound at week 2 showed right subclavian vein thrombosis and soft-tissue hematoma.
objective.advanced_workup: Neck ultrasound and thoracic CT excluded deep cervical or thoracic abscesses. Chin/submandibular skin biopsy showed nonspecific putrid inflammation without leukemic cutis. Bone marrow biopsy and cytogenetics confirmed myelodysplastic syndrome with refractory anemia and excess blasts II (MDS RAEB-II) with 10% marrow blasts, atypical trilineage dysplasia, and karyotype 46,XY with dual translocations t(2;12)(p13;q13) and t(6;9)(p22;q34).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Severe generalized herpes zoster (zoster generalisatus) complicated by Pseudomonas aeruginosa superinfection, right subclavian vein thrombosis, anaphylactic shock to intravenous varicella-zoster immunoglobulin, and fatal septic shock in an HIV-negative 64-year-old man with newly diagnosed high-risk myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS RAEB-II with 10% marrow blasts, 11% peripheral blasts, and t(2;12)(p13;q13) and t(6;9)(p22;q34)). Despite escalation to high-dose IV acyclovir (1,000 mg every 8 hours), piperacillin, levofloxacin, oral vancomycin, RBC/platelet transfusions, and cytoreductive therapy with azacitidine, the patient suffered anaphylactic shock during IV varicella immunoglobulin infusion and died 6 days later of refractory septic shock.
